wizards.title: Prompt, RAG, long context or fine-tune?
wizards.blurb: Four questions to pick how to give a model what it lacks.

need.q: What is missing when the model gets it wrong?
options: Knowledge it doesn’t have: private, recent or citable facts
Behavior: format, tone or a narrow skill
Probably nothing: the instructions are unclear

k1.q: How big is the knowledge, and how often does it change?
options: Small and stable: a few documents

k2.q: Do answers need citations or per-user permissions, or is the corpus huge?
options: No, and a few documents per question are enough

b1.q: Can a handful of examples in the prompt teach it?
options: No, or it must run cheaply at very high volume

r-prompt.why: Write the task as a clear spec with examples and structure, then measure on an eval set.

r-longctx.result: Put the documents in context, with prompt caching
r-longctx.why: A small, stable corpus fits in the window; cache it as a stable prefix and skip retrieval.

r-rag.why: Retrieve the right passages per question, filter by permissions and cite sources.

r-examples.why: Show diverse examples and let the API enforce the format.

r-finetune.why: Narrow, high-volume behavior is where fine-tuning pays. Build the eval before the training set.

wizards.title: Workflow or agent?
wizards.blurb: Decide whether code or the model should choose the next step.

w1.q: Can you write the steps down in advance?
options: No, they depend on what we find

w2.q: Do different inputs need different handling?

a1.q: Is a wrong action expensive or irreversible?

r-routing.why: Classify the input, then run a specialized chain per type.

r-chain.result: A prompt chain with code gates
r-chain.why: Fixed steps, checked by code between them.

r-agent-hitl.result: An agent with approvals and tight permissions
r-agent-hitl.why: Let the model choose steps, but gate side effects behind human approval and least privilege.

r-agent.why: Give it good tools, a step and cost budget, and evals on trajectories.

wizards.title: Single agent or multi-agent?
wizards.blurb: Check whether splitting the work will actually help.

m1.q: Does one agent’s context overflow or degrade on this task?

m3.q: Would independent parallel work make it much faster?

m2.q: Are the subtasks independent and wide, or tightly coupled and deep?
options: Independent and wide, such as broad research
Tightly coupled, such as one refactor

r-single.why: No overflow and no parallelism to gain: extra agents add cost and coordination failures.

r-single-ctx.result: One agent with better context management, plus read-only helpers
r-single-ctx.why: Keep writes in one agent; use subagents only for search or review, and compact context.

r-multi.why: Fan out with clear briefs, return summaries, budget tokens per agent and evaluate the whole system.

wizards.title: Which vector store?
wizards.blurb: Pick a vector store from what you already run and how much you want to operate.

v1.q: What do you already run in production?

v2.q: Is your corpus under tens of millions of vectors with moderate query load?
options: No, or we expect huge growth

v3.q: Do you want to operate the infrastructure yourselves?
options: No, we want a managed service

r-pgvector.why: Least new infrastructure, transactional updates and SQL filters; benchmark recall at your size.

r-search.result: Use your search engine’s vector support
r-search.why: Hybrid search is natural when keyword search already lives there.

r-managed.why: Compare on filtering, hybrid search, multi-tenancy and cost model; see the matrix.

r-selfhost.why: Plan for backups, upgrades, sharding and monitoring; see the matrix.

wizards.title: API or self-hosting?
wizards.blurb: Decide where your model should run.

s1.q: Must data stay inside your own environment?

s3.q: Is traffic high and steady enough to keep GPUs busy most of the day?
options: No, it is bursty or modest

s2.q: Does an open-weight model pass your eval?

r-api.why: Pay per token, keep a second provider ready and use caching and batch discounts.

r-selfhost.why: Size memory with the VRAM planner, pick a serving engine, and measure goodput against your latency target.

r-private.result: A frontier model through a private deployment
r-private.why: Cloud platforms and zero-data-retention terms can meet residency needs when open models fall short.

wizards.title: Which eval method?
wizards.blurb: Pick the cheapest grader that measures what you care about.

e1.q: Can a program check the output?

e2.q: Is the criterion specific and answerable with pass or fail?
options: No, it is broad, like overall quality

e3.q: Do you have human labels to calibrate a judge against?

r-code.why: Fast, free and exact. Use them wherever they apply.

r-split.why: Use error analysis to break “quality” into specific failure modes, then grade each one.

r-judge.why: Measure its true positive and true negative rates on held-out labels before trusting it.

r-label.why: Human labels are the ground truth a judge is checked against.

wizards.title: MCP server, plain function or skill?
wizards.blurb: Choose how to give an agent a new capability or procedure.

c1.q: Is it a capability (an action or data access) or a procedure (how to do something)?

c2.q: Will more than one app, agent or team use it?

r-skill.why: A folder with a SKILL.md file: instructions and scripts loaded only when relevant.

r-mcp.why: One server works in every compliant host, with standard discovery and auth.

r-function.result: Define a plain tool in your own code
r-function.why: No protocol needed for a single application’s own functions.
